article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Lactoferrin has two ferric-iron binding sites, one per lobe.
boundary: Source1 Abstract identifies ligands; source2 Abstract specifies Fe(III)/carbonate. Binding is not excretion.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Apolactoferrin's crystal structure contains an open N-lobe and closed unliganded C-lobe.
boundary: Abstract; do not convert a crystal conformation into universal solution behavior.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Lactoferrin caused LPS release and altered bacterial outer-membrane permeability under tested conditions.
setting: E. coli mutant and Salmonella Typhimurium in buffer assays
boundary: Abstract: iron saturation blocked LPS release; chemistry-sensitive effect, not clinical bactericidal efficacy.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Lactoferrin inhibited P. aeruginosa biofilm development at exposure below growth inhibition through iron-linked twitching behavior.
boundary: Publisher Abstract and Figures1–4 captions; formation endpoint does not establish clearance of mature infection.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Functional LbpA enabled N. gonorrhoeae to use lactoferrin-bound iron in the reported experiments.
boundary: Abstract: loss of LbpA abolished use; clinical isolate heterogeneity precludes species-wide certainty.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Negatively charged LbpB regions protected meningococci against lactoferricin in killing assays.
boundary: Figures1,4–8; stability/export controls, but washing removed shed protein and affected assay protection.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Lactoferrin antimicrobial surfaces show signatures of recurrent positive selection in primates.
boundary: Figures1–3; evolutionary-conflict interpretation, not direct identification of every selective agent.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Reconstructed lactoferricin peptides differed in microbial growth, viability, and membrane effects.
setting: Synthesized peptides and defined bacterial strains
boundary: Figures2–6; ancestral inference and isolated-peptide assays do not measure oral intact-protein exposure.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Gastric recovery was numerically higher for holoLF than low-saturation lactoferrin, but the difference was not statistically significant.
boundary: Results/Discussion: P = 0.09. This numerical trend does not establish an iron-saturation effect; gastric recovery is not systemic uptake or efficacy.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Both groups improved hematological measures, with abdominal-pain and constipation scores favoring lactoferrin in the pregnancy trial.
boundary: TablesI–II; no noninferiority margin; reported between-group nonsignificance needs reconciliation with Hb table.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: The pediatric IBD trial reported improved iron indices and lower IL-6 and hepcidin-25 with lactoferrin.
boundary: Table2; Figure1 documents attrition. Biomarker shifts do not establish microbial mediation; side-effect discontinuation reporting conflicts.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: ELFIN did not demonstrate a reduction in late-onset infection with its enteral bovine lactoferrin regimen.
boundary: Abstract Findings: adjusted RR0.95, 95%CI0.86–1.04. This is application-specific contrary evidence, not a test of all formulations.

article: Lactoferrin: iron withholding and microbial countermeasures
claim: Microbial response may depend jointly on available iron-binding capacity and active protein or peptide exposure.
boundary: Editorial synthesis. Iron restoration and peptide depletion must distinguish the predicted contributions; no human benefit is inferred.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Hepcidin binding promotes ferroportin internalization and decreases cellular iron export.
boundary: Abstract supports direct mechanism; not a human whole-body iron-removal result.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Hepcidin occupies ferroportin's outward-facing transport pathway.
boundary: Abstract and figure descriptions; cobalt was the structural iron mimic. Transport assays support functional interpretation.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: IL-6 administration increased urinary hepcidin and reduced circulating iron in healthy volunteers.
boundary: Figure4 and Human studies Methods; urinary hepcidin is not a serum measurement and hypoferremia is not chronic anemia.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Loss of erythroferrone impaired rapid hepcidin suppression and anemia recovery after blood loss in mice.
boundary: Abstract and Figures3,5–6 descriptions; source correction concerns supplementary primers, not revised biological conclusions.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Salmonella-associated ferroportin downregulation persisted in hepcidin-deficient mice.
boundary: Figure4; does not establish a particular pathogen effector or universal infection response.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Hepcidin-mediated hypoferremia improved defense against V. vulnificus in the studied mice.
setting: Hepcidin deficiency and agonist mouse comparisons
boundary: Results: serum availability separated from liver stores; not a human treatment trial or direct antimicrobial peptide mechanism.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Hepcidin protection against NTBI-responsive infection was strain- and model-dependent.
setting: Mouse Yersinia, S. aureus and M. tuberculosis comparisons
boundary: Figures1–3 and NTBI results; O9 differed from O8. Negative findings constrain a universal extracellular/intracellular rule.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Higher ferroportin expression limited intracellular Salmonella multiplication in the tested host cells.
boundary: Figures1–4; iron-response reporters support deprivation, with possible indirect effects and specific host-cell background.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Hepcidin increased cytosolic iron while reducing inferred vacuolar iron and antimicrobial oxidant responses in the Lim models.
boundary: Figures3–4; reporter inference is not an absolute chemical assay. Mechanism must not be generalized to every intracellular pathogen.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Iron restriction, suppressed erythropoiesis, and shortened erythrocyte survival contributed to inflammatory anemia in mice.
boundary: Abstract; no ongoing microbial replication. Does not quantify each mechanism in human patients.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: An exploratory rheumatoid arthritis trial analysis found early hepcidin decline and later hemoglobin improvement with IL-6 receptor blockade.
boundary: Figures1–2/Table1; multimechanism treatment and correlations cannot prove exclusive hepcidin mediation.

article: Hepcidin and ferroportin: iron redistribution in host defense
claim: Erythroid recovery may remain delayed after iron export recovers from prolonged inflammatory exposure.
boundary: Testable synthesis, not an established human result. Full rescue by matched iron delivery would weaken the proposed persistent component.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: Macrophage erythrocyte recycling supplies iron back to plasma and supports new red-cell production.
boundary: Review sections Iron Homeostasis and Recovery of Iron from Erythrocytes; this homeostatic role alone does not establish pathogen-driven selection.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: Transferrin substitutions at rapidly evolving sites alter recognition by bacterial TbpA.
setting: Recombinant transferrin and heterologously expressed bacterial receptors
boundary: Figures 1–3; binding phenotypes and evolutionary analyses do not directly quantify clinical infection risk.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: NCOA4 depletion impairs ferritin degradation and alters cellular iron-response markers.
boundary: Figure 3 and Extended Data Figures 7–10; iron loading and chelation experiments, not microbial delivery measurements.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: Myeloid Fth loss worsened Salmonella outcomes after iron loading, with no baseline survival difference.
boundary: Figures 1–2; distinguish genetic buffering failure plus experimental loading from ordinary human supplementation.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: IRP-deficient macrophages accumulated ferritin iron that was mobilized as Salmonella acquired radioiron.
setting: IRP1/IRP2-deficient murine macrophages infected with S. Typhimurium ATCC 14028s
boundary: Figure 4E supports an accessible reservoir; direct mobilization machinery was not identified. IRP loss also changes lipocalin-2 and cytokine responses.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: CD163 mediates endocytosis of haptoglobin–hemoglobin complexes.
boundary: Abstract only read; no infection efficacy claim.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: LRP/CD91 mediates uptake of hemopexin–heme complexes.
boundary: Abstract and indexed Results excerpts; receptor route is not proof of pathogen starvation.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: HxuA mutants can separate hemopexin binding from heme acquisition.
setting: Rabbit hemopexin and reconstructed Hxu transport in E. coli
boundary: Figures 4–5; the M-loop deletion retained binding but failed acquisition. Do not relabel the growth model as human infection.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: S. aureus Newman preferentially acquired hemoglobin-derived over transferrin-derived iron in the tested culture.
boundary: Table 1; preference varied with growth phase. Hemopexin did not support growth in Figure 1.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: HO-1 protected against experimental malaria liver injury without lowering parasitemia in principal comparisons.
boundary: Figures 1–3; a disease-tolerance result, not universal antiparasitic activity.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: Inflammation affects ferritin interpretation, and ferritin alone cannot establish iron overload.
boundary: WHO recommendations 1.4 and 4.1–4.2; these are biomarker interpretation boundaries, not evidence that ferritin quantifies microbial access.

article: Transferrin, ferritin and the race to recycle heme
claim: Host heme-clearance kinetics may predict protection better than carrier concentration alone.
setting: Proposed sterile human-cell and cell-free comparisons
boundary: Hypothesis, not an established result. Protection fully explained by extracellular binding would weaken a requirement for cellular clearance; no microbial-access conclusion follows alone.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: GSH supports peroxide-reducing enzymes and can be regenerated from GSSG using NADPH.
boundary: Review biochemical framework; Yang Figures 1–5 establish GPX4-specific cell-death relationships rather than universal mitochondrial protection.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: GSH coordinates Cu(I) under controlled solution conditions.
boundary: Spectrophotometric–potentiometric titrations and phosphorescence; chemical speciation is not a measured excretion effect.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Depleting GSH reduced initial CTR1-associated copper uptake in cultured cells.
boundary: Figures 4–6; rescue supports a GSH role but does not imply all cell types or whole-body copper balance respond identically.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: SLC25A39 loss can lower mitochondrial GSH without reducing whole-cell GSH.
setting: Human cell lines and isolated mitochondria
boundary: Figure 2; genetic perturbation and isotope uptake. No routine drug exposure.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: SLC25A39 and SLC25A37 interact in support of mitochondrial function.
setting: K562 cells in defined metabolic media
boundary: Figures 3–5; environment-dependent genetic interaction, not a clinical exposure association.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: AFG3L2-mediated SLC25A39 turnover participates in GSH-responsive feedback.
boundary: Figures 1–4; iron–sulfur-associated regulatory interpretation remains bounded to the tested system.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Copper-dependent death can involve lipoylated protein aggregation and Fe–S protein loss.
setting: Human cancer cell models with mouse comparison
boundary: Figures 4–6; GSH depletion arm is experimental. Verified erratum 10.1126/science.abq4855 concerns Figure 4C, Table S2 completeness and a figure callout; no correction to the cited GSH/lipoylation findings is described. Coordinator provenance records the notice.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Acute cell exposure and subchronic rat exposure produced different GSH patterns.
setting: Rat proximal-tubule cells and Fischer 344 rats
boundary: Abstract only; differing models/routes prevent treating the contrast as a matched longitudinal experiment.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Busulfan parent-drug metabolism prominently uses GSH conjugation.
setting: Official human pharmacology and human liver enzyme study
boundary: Label section 12.3; Gibbs abstract. The APAP interaction in section 7.1 is conditional, not quantified here.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Acetaminophen mainly undergoes glucuronidation/sulfation; GSH detoxifies NAPQI.
boundary: Label Metabolism and Excretion; does not mean GSH is the main parent-clearance route.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Acetaminophen is not conventionally classified as an NSAID.
boundary: FDA brochure separates acetaminophen from NSAIDs; classification claim rather than an intervention.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Some ALT elevations resolved during continued therapeutic acetaminophen administration without measured liver dysfunction.
boundary: Results/Figures 2–4; no direct GSH or metal measurements, exclusion criteria limit generalization.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Diclofenac can produce reactive intermediates trapped as GSH conjugates.
setting: Rat bile and human hepatocyte cultures
boundary: Abstract only; does not demonstrate ordinary-use depletion or a class-wide NSAID effect.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: ADH/ALDH oxidation is distinct from chronic ethanol-associated effects on mitochondrial GSH and CYP2E1 stress.
setting: Human metabolic framework; rat and mouse mechanistic studies
boundary: Official metabolism page plus primary-study abstracts. Humanized CYP2E1 mice are not a human intervention; no inference of ethanol GSH-conjugation clearance.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: Toxic acetaminophen exposure can mobilize chelatable iron toward mitochondria and amplify injury.
setting: Fasted male C57BL/6 primary mouse hepatocytes; 10 mM culture APAP
boundary: Figures 2–4; indirect probes and pharmacological interventions. Not human therapeutic exposure.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: GSH can activate the Listeria PrfA virulence regulator.
setting: L. monocytogenes 10403S background and infection models
boundary: Figures 1–4 and Methods; strain/pathogen-specific evidence, not a generic microbiome prediction.

article: Glutathione, metals and the mitochondrial reserve
claim: A drug–metal interaction could depend on limited mitochondrial GSH delivery rather than total-cell depletion.
boundary: Editorial synthesis; no cited study establishes the full clinical co-exposure chain. Import restoration, metal timing and matched drug metabolism are required discriminators.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: BSEP-mediated bile-salt transport is distinct from metal-associated cargo export.
setting: Rat transporter in oocytes and Sf9 vesicles
boundary: Abstract; no metal transport or metal-binding endpoint.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: ATP7B trafficking and lysosomal exocytosis contribute to canalicular copper handling.
setting: HepG2, other cell models and mouse experiments
boundary: Figures 1–7; canalicular-cyst copper is not human fecal clearance.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Historical biliary copper studies made different ligand assignments.
setting: Human and rat bile; electrophoresis and chromatography
boundary: Abstracts only; method-dependent evidence. Modern native speciation is needed to reconcile the assignments.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Biliary copper reabsorption is generally limited under usual physiology.
boundary: Section 3.1.4; avoids generalizing methylmercury return to every metal.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Mrp2 and GSH were required for substantial biliary arsenic recovery in the tested rat model.
boundary: Figure 1 and Table II; collected bile/speciation, not intact-gut human elimination.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Methylmercury–GSH transport was ATP-independent in isolated rat canalicular vesicles.
boundary: Abstract; does not identify a universal MRP2 route.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: MRP2 handled tested mercury–cysteine species, with nonuniform fecal differences in rats.
setting: Human MRP2 vesicles and Wistar/TR− rats
boundary: Figures 7–9; plain methylmercury chloride fecal difference was not significant; no bile collection.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Changing bile flow did not necessarily change absolute GSH/methylmercury secretion.
boundary: Abstract; distinguishes fluid volume from cargo flux.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Host GGT-dependent processing facilitated methylmercury return in the guinea-pig biliary model.
boundary: Abstract; biliary-tree return, not microbial BSH or human treatment.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Biliary mercury underwent intestinal reabsorption in rats.
boundary: Abstract; author did not establish repeated enterohepatic cycling.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: B. thetaiotaomicron BSH manipulation changed bile-acid composition without testing metal clearance.
boundary: Figures 2–4; bile-salt substrate specificity, mouse muricholate context.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Microbiota influenced methylmercury elimination but no single candidate explained the whole effect.
setting: Humanized and microbiota-depleted mice; human observations
boundary: Figures 2–5; human association is not causal; single-species and prebiotic findings were qualified.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Diet and antibiotic perturbations altered mercury elimination in mice.
boundary: Abstract; interventions also affect host physiology.

article: Bile, metal export and the route back
claim: Microbial bile-acid remodeling could change net metal loss through transport, speciation or return.
setting: Proposed integrated liver–gut and gnotobiotic experiments
boundary: Editorial synthesis; each link and overall mass balance require measurement, including a null outcome.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Vancomycin recognizes appropriate D-Ala-D-Ala-containing precursor peptides.
boundary: Primary abstract: complex formation and specificity tests. Zinc contribution was not tested.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Vancomycin exposure induced zinc-responsive transcription in the tested bacterial cultures.
boundary: Figure2 and Methods. Transcription does not establish lethal zinc depletion.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Vancomycin bound Zn(II) weakly in the specified buffered assay.
boundary: Figure3c: Kd1,220±479µM. Conditional assay affinity, not an intracellular constant.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Zinc potentiation depended on the tested resistance and precursor context.
setting: Resistant/susceptible bacterial pairs and engineered S.coelicolor
boundary: Figures1,3. Laboratory cultures; no human or animal infection efficacy test.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Zinc-associated vancomycin polymers were supported by structural assays.
setting: Purified drug crystallography and fibre diffraction
boundary: Figure4 and supplementary Figure9. Does not establish target-bound polymers at infection sites.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: An engineered dipicolyl-vancomycin conjugate added pyrophosphate recognition.
boundary: Primary abstract. Cannot assign derivative behavior to unmodified vancomycin.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: VanNHdipi inhibited tested metallo-β-lactamases and potentiated carbapenems in selected isolates.
boundary: Tables2–3,Figure5; zinc reversal described with FigureS5. Exact zinc coordination/extraction mechanism remains unresolved.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: A bacitracin structure contains zinc and a pyrophosphate ligand.
boundary: Primary abstract; shortened target analogue, not an intact bacterial membrane.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: PBT2 mediated zinc/proton exchange in artificial membranes.
boundary: Figure3. Bacterial metal accumulation was assessed separately in Figure2; transport is distinct from nutrient sequestration.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Iron-depleted growth increased cefiderocol uptake in PAO1.
setting: Radiolabeled uptake after controlled medium exposure
boundary: Figure2 and Table1. Drug-entry evidence, not proof of killing by iron starvation.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Gallium disrupted P.aeruginosa iron uptake and PvdS-related signaling.
setting: Culture uptake and inducible pvdS experiments
boundary: Figures4–7. Contributions vary with iron supply; not a universal single-enzyme mechanism.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Gallium increased several virulence-associated products in three tested P.aeruginosa strains.
setting: PA14 and two selected CF isolates in culture
boundary: Figure1;10/25µM gallium experiments and time-dependent biofilm assays. Not a demonstration of worsened disease in patients.

article: Vancomycin and zinc: starvation, assembly and resistance
claim: Local zinc availability may determine whether nutrient restriction or drug assembly dominates.
setting: Proposed cross-study evidence appraisal and observational interpretation
boundary: Editorial synthesis. Zinc-responsive signaling, metal availability, assembly and biological outcome are separate evidentiary levels; agreement does not alone establish causation.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Silybin forms Fe(III) complexes in the tested chemical systems.
boundary: Abstract; Experimental and Infrared spectra excerpts. No aqueous plasma affinity or human clearance established.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Dehydrosilybin showed stronger Fe/Cu chelation than several parent flavonolignans in comparative assays.
boundary: Abstract and Results screening excerpt; assay competition and oxidation state matter.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Electrochemical and fluorescence measurements supported silybin–copper complex formation.
boundary: Abstract; full experimental conditions not accessed. Nickel-specific behavior is not inferred.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Dehydroflavonolignans did not suppress iron Fenton chemistry despite protection in a copper erythrocyte assay.
setting: Cell-free reactions and isolated rat erythrocytes.
boundary: Results 3.3–3.4, Figures 9–11; distinct endpoints, neither demonstrates human toxicity or benefit.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Oral milk-thistle extract improved injury markers during injected nickel-sulfate exposure.
setting: Male Wistar rats, renal and liver studies.
boundary: 2017 Abstract; 2018 Methods and Results. No Ni complex identification or excretion balance; prevention/co-exposure rather than treatment of established human poisoning.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Silymarin lowered blood lead less than DMSA in the tested rat co-exposure model.
setting: Lead acetate in drinking water for eight weeks.
boundary: Table 1; blood concentration is not total burden. No demonstrated excretion pathway.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Vitamin C plus silymarin improved liver endpoints during dietary lead exposure.
boundary: Abstract; no silymarin-only arm, so single-agent attribution is unsupported.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: The tested Legalon Forte preparation reduced the postmeal serum-iron rise in a small crossover.
boundary: Methods and Figure 1; indirect absorption endpoint over four hours. No long-term unloading or excretion measurement.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Ferritin decreased in a silybin–phosphatidylcholine dose-ranging study without significant iron or transferrin-saturation change.
boundary: Abstract Results; no placebo arm described; tissue stores were not directly measured.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Oral silymarin did not improve the primary ALT outcome, HCV RNA or quality of life over placebo.
setting: 154 previously treated chronic HCV patients, 24 weeks.
boundary: Abstract Results and study outcomes; does not evaluate a metal-selected subgroup or every formulation.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: NASH activity-score response was not significantly improved; secondary fibrosis outcomes favored silymarin.
boundary: Abstract Results and Conclusions; secondary findings need confirmation and do not establish metal mediation.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Oral silybin A/B exposure increased nonlinearly across dose cohorts.
boundary: Abstract Results; exposure does not itself prove efficacy.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Dehydroflavonolignans bound zinc and inhibited isolated enzymes, with chelation alone insufficient to explain all effects.
setting: Yeast/equine ADH, bovine GDH and docking.
boundary: Figures 8–12, 19–21 and Discussion; not a whole-organism microbial or human alcohol-clearance result.

article: Silymarin, metal binding and the liver
claim: Changed intestinal metal speciation could have different implications for host uptake and microbial access.
setting: Conceptual interpretation of intestinal chemical and host-absorption evidence.
boundary: Editorial synthesis; existing binding and absorption findings do not establish microbiome mediation or the direction of microbial metal access.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Boulardii isolates lie within S. cerevisiae diversity near wine-associated strains in comparative genomic analysis.
setting: Genome comparisons, not a metal assay
boundary: Taxonomic position section and Figure 4; relatedness does not establish identical binding performance.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: The lead study used MYA-796, independently documented as a boulardii-derived isolate.
boundary: Stathatou Methods, Yeast strain; Batista Genome Announcement. Supports identity, not efficacy of a retail formulation.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Inactive MYA-796 captures Pb(II) from water, with cell-wall chemistry implicated.
boundary: Figure 2 and spectroscopy/discussion; no host clearance endpoint or proof every cell was dead.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Free and immobilized S. cerevisiae preparations adsorbed Pb(II), with microscopy implicating the wall.
boundary: Abstract only; strain and viability details not verified. Not assigned to boulardii.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: The tested yeast strains removed less than 10% inorganic arsenic from solution despite some transport effects.
setting: In vitro As(III)/As(V), digestion and intestinal-cell assays
boundary: Abstract and conclusions snippets; mechanism of transport change is not resolved, and the rice result highlighted was bacterial.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Yeast-associated reductions in mercury bioaccessibility did not extend to all food matrices.
setting: Simulated digestion of Hg(II), methylmercury and foods
boundary: Abstract and supplementary Tables S1–S2: Ultralevura included in swordfish comparison; BY4741 used for ligand competition. Neither is a human elimination trial.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: ATCC 9763 metal retention changed with pretreatment and digestion, including release under some conditions.
setting: Mixed-metal aqueous model followed by simulated digestion
boundary: Methods 2.3–2.7 and Figure 1. Another strain; source has numerical/pretreatment inconsistencies, so no optimized percentage is generalized.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Acr3 and Ycf1 confer distinct arsenite-resistance routes in laboratory yeast.
setting: S. cerevisiae mutants and radiotracer/membrane-vesicle assays
boundary: Figures 1–3; exclusion versus vacuolar sequestration does not establish the net behavior of ingested boulardii.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: A boulardii preparation improved selected redox and hematologic measures in arsenate-exposed rats.
setting: Male Wistar rats, oral co-treatment, 28 days
boundary: Journal abstract only; no strain accession or metal-balance endpoint there. Docking does not measure arsenic binding.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Administered S. boulardii was recovered in human feces, and ampicillin altered recovery.
boundary: Abstract; fecal yeast recovery is not fecal metal recovery or reduced body burden.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: S. boulardii use was associated with Saccharomyces infections in a hospital registry study.
boundary: Results and Discussion limitations; retrospective association, no general-user absolute risk and incomplete probiotic/isolate matching.

article: Can probiotic yeast carry metals out of the gut?
claim: Durable wall retention could reduce intestinal metal delivery independently of viable yeast metabolism.
setting: Conceptual synthesis of published retention, transport and host-outcome evidence
boundary: Would weaken with desorption, analytical losses or a transport benefit explained solely by barrier changes. No clinical efficacy is claimed.
